subject: The Cultivation No-Dig bed, depicted in mid-July

generation.prompt:
Edit the first reference, the approved square “Start growing” no-dig bed picture, into the follow-up photographic illustration for a British gardening book, about eight weeks later in early summer. The first reference governs the garden, camera direction and identity, orientation and size of the bed. The second reference is a genuine garden photo to use only for the scale, leaf shapes, irregular spacing, overlapping foliage and stage of grown lettuce and beetroot. Do not copy its different view, hoops, white edging, or neighbouring beds.

The photograph explains the size of a manageable first plot. Make the single original rectangular ground-level no-dig bed the main subject, from its front edge and two grey corner blocks to its far end, with both long edges legible and all four corners inside the frame. Keep the original approximate 1.2 m physical width, long narrow shape, dark compost with grass paths on both sides, original oblique view with the near short edge broad in the foreground and the far end towards the right of the glasshouse. Frame the bed large enough to read when printed around 66 mm wide. Extend the view to a landscape 3:2 composition by allowing extra space on the sides and, if needed, stepping back slightly from the same camera position. Include a little grass in front of the grey blocks and a continuous small margin around the whole bed. The existing angled aluminium glasshouse on its low masonry base, blue shed glimpse at left, small terracotta pots, fence and black water butt stay recognisable and in their original relative positions. The small bare and timber-edged growing areas visible behind the main plot must not read as other beds. Show mown grass continuing behind the far end in front of the fence, and a little perimeter shrub foliage, keeping the foreground vegetable bed the only defined soil bed. Retain low leafy shrubs around the perimeter in a natural way.

Completely remove the kneeling gardener, his hands, the empty/part-filled module tray and all traces of his clothing. Replace his footprint in the view with the accessible grass path and the actual original bed edge. The bed is now planted along its whole length. Grow the five green lettuce plugs visible across the near end into recognisable well established heads of loose green butterhead lettuce, individually shaped, some tighter and some broader, slightly off-centre in their row. Behind them use a couple of staggered short rows of the same lettuces or deeper green spinach in the previously bare middle. Retain established beetroot with beet-red petioles and green to burgundy-veined broad leaves in the middle-to-far part; established deep green spinach with plain soft oval leaves at the far end. These are plausible home garden plants after about two months, with ordinary small exposed patches of dark compost between the groups. Get cultivar-specific leaf anatomy and natural scale, not supermarket spheres, perfectly repeated rosettes, synchronized rows or a completely uniform carpet of leaves. A few partly-picked or nibbled edges and irregular overlaps are enough. Preserve clear grassy strips along both sides so the viewer can see the width. No people, extra beds, edging around the whole bed, hoops, stakes, labels, text, or added props. Natural diffuse late-spring/early-summer British daylight with believable colours and readable midtones. One grounded, candid, photographic image.

Edit this exact photograph of the established “Start growing” bed for a book. This reference already contains the correct low timber planter on the left. Keep and clearly show that planter in its original spot against the greenhouse/shed, with the same timber sides, modest dimensions, and existing shrub. Use the original geometry of the main ground-level no-dig bed, grass paths and greenhouse. No person. The date depicted is now mid-July in Cornwall. 

Remove the two light-grey concrete bricks at the front corners of the main soil bed entirely. Reveal slightly unruly grass and textured no-dig soil at those spots, meeting in an unedged, irregular but legible front bed line. The low masonry foundation under the distant greenhouse stays. Make the main crop bed a little tattier in an ordinary, believable way: the established front lettuces are different sizes and less evenly aligned, with one or two visibly picked around the edges, an old lower leaf near the soil, an occasional bite and a small gap where a lettuce was harvested. Keep reasonable plant spacing. The beetroot leaves have varied spread and lean, a few scuffed lower leaves, more visible soil between a couple of plants. At the far end there is uneven established spinach with one taller plant beginning to go to seed, while the greater part of the bed remains productive. No widespread disease or distress. Add a couple of small incidental weeds and a few grass blades from the lawn at the border, as in a well-used home grower's bed. Keep leaf forms recognisable and low enough that the full outline of the bed can be understood. 

Advance the rest of the garden to mid-July too: the deciduous shrub in the timber planter has natural, somewhat irregular green summer foliage over the existing reddish woody framework, no mass of bare winter stems and no showy new flowers. The plants in the two existing terracotta pots have grown into modest leafy plants. Through the glass, show lightly visible, taller leafy midsummer greenhouse growth, with the window frames and reflections still clear. The rest of the backdrop is gently leafier, within the existing shrub positions. Keep the lawn, aluminium greenhouse and its footprint, the fence, water butt, and blue shed identifiable. Avoid introducing another bed or any new garden structure. Quiet natural midsummer daylight with readable detail and restrained green saturation.

Crop in modestly to centre the main bed more strongly, putting less emphasis on the left lawn and the space above the bed. Keep a horizontal 3:2 image for the existing book layout, with the same camera direction and natural perspective. Retain enough of the left timber planter to clearly recognise it, and all four corners and edges of the main ground-level bed inside the frame. Both grass paths, and a little grass beyond the near and far edges, should still show the length and reach of the bed. Think a small step nearer or a modest tighter focal length, not a close-up or a different garden. The planted bed should dominate the photo. Make it feel like a candid real British garden photograph, not a staged demonstration.
